title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds
strapline: The language of chemistry: symbols, formulae and what a compound really is.
bigIdea: There are about a hundred kinds of atom. Everything else is those atoms joined in different combinations — and chemists write that down in a precise, international shorthand.
priorKnowledge: Year 7: substances are made of particles.
Unit 1: pure substances and mixtures; conservation of mass observed on the balance.
futureLearning: GCSE: sub-atomic particles, electronic structure, ionic and covalent bonding, relative formula mass and moles.

misconceptions.misconception: A compound is just a very well-mixed mixture.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Both look uniform, and both involve more than one substance.
misconceptions.addressIt: Iron and sulfur demo: separate the mixture with a magnet, then heat to form iron sulfide and show the magnet no longer works. Properties changed, so it is a new substance.

misconceptions.misconception: The symbol 'Co' means carbon and oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils read symbols as letters rather than as units.
misconceptions.addressIt: Drill capital-letter-starts-a-new-element explicitly; contrast CO with Co on the board every time formulae are written.

misconceptions.misconception: Mass is lost when a reaction gives off a gas, or gained when a metal burns.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils trust the balance and do not count invisible gases.
misconceptions.addressIt: Repeat the reaction in a sealed flask; explicitly account for every atom before and after.

misconceptions.misconception: Atoms of an element are all slightly different, like grains of sand.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Everyday particles are irregular, so pupils generalise.
misconceptions.addressIt: State and enforce that all atoms of an element are the same kind; use identical counters in modelling, never varied ones.

keyVocabulary.definition: The smallest particle of an element that can exist.
A substance made of only one type of atom; it cannot be broken down chemically.
Two or more different elements chemically bonded together in fixed proportions.
Two or more atoms chemically bonded together.
The symbols and numbers showing which atoms, and how many of each, are in a substance.
The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants, because atoms are only rearranged.

practicals.title: Iron and sulfur: mixture then compound
control: Fume cupboard or very well ventilated room; use minimal quantities
Teacher demonstration only; heat until the glow starts then remove the flame

practicals.title: Conservation of mass in a sealed and open vessel
hazards: Pressure build-up in a sealed flask
control: Goggles; use a balloon rather than a tight bung, or loosen after reading

formative: Element-or-compound card sort with formulae, timed.
Whiteboard drill: how many atoms of each element in Ca(NO3)2?
Hinge question after Lesson 3 to decide whether to reteach formula reading.

summative.title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds quiz
summative.style: 20 marks, 25 minutes, sat in the last 25 minutes of Lesson 6.
summative.markSchemeNotes: No credit for 'it got heavier' without reference to atoms joining with oxygen from the air.

lessons.title: The atomic model and how it changed
objectives: Describe Dalton's model of the atom
Explain how scientific models change when new evidence appears
retrieval: What is in the gaps between particles?

sequence.detail: Five questions recalling Unit 1.
Dalton's four ideas, stated simply; brief timeline from Greek ideas to Dalton, emphasising evidence not opinion.
Timeline annotation task: for each step, what evidence forced the change?
Discussion: 'Was Dalton wrong?' — introduce the idea of a model being useful rather than true.

keyQuestions: What makes an idea scientific rather than just an opinion?
Which parts of Dalton's model do we still use?
support: Timeline cards pre-cut with dates supplied.
challenge: Research and summarise one piece of evidence that later showed atoms are divisible.
lessons.homework: Write 100 words: why do scientists change their models?
lessons.exitTicket: State one thing Dalton got right and one thing later found to be wrong.

lessons.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
objectives: Classify substances as elements, compounds or mixtures from diagrams and formulae
Explain why a compound has different properties from its elements

sequence.detail: Particle diagram classification on whiteboards, five diagrams.
Iron and sulfur: test the mixture with a magnet, heat to form iron sulfide, retest. Record properties in a before/after table.
Define compound formally; contrast with mixture on three criteria: bonding, proportions, separation.
Card sort with 18 substances, then write three justifications in full sentences.
Hinge question and reteach if under 80 per cent correct.

keyQuestions: Why does the magnet stop working after heating?
Is air an element, compound or mixture? Justify.
challenge: Explain why the ratio of iron to sulfur matters in the compound but not in the mixture.
lessons.homework: Classify 12 everyday substances and justify three of them.
lessons.exitTicket: Give two differences between a mixture and a compound.

lessons.title: Symbols and formulae
objectives: Recall the symbols for the first 20 elements and common metals
Read a chemical formula to state the number of atoms of each element
retrieval: Element, compound or mixture: three quick diagrams
Why does a compound have new properties?

sequence.detail: Quick-fire symbols known from prior years.
Rules for symbols (one capital, optional lower case); rules for reading subscripts and brackets. Model Ca(NO3)2 fully.
I do / we do / you do on six formulae of increasing difficulty, including brackets.
Formula decoding worksheet, 15 items, self-marked from the board.
Symbol drill — 20 elements against the clock, recorded for a personal best.

keyQuestions: What is the difference between CO and Co?
How many atoms in total are in Ca(NO3)2?
support: Periodic table with the 20 required symbols highlighted; brackets questions withheld until the basic set is secure.
challenge: Write the formula from a name for six ionic compounds using a supplied ion table.
lessons.homework: Learn the 20 element symbols; short self-quiz sheet.
lessons.exitTicket: State the number of each type of atom in Mg(OH)2.

lessons.title: Conservation of mass
objectives: State the law of conservation of mass
Explain apparent mass changes in open systems
Use atom counts to justify a balanced equation

sequence.detail: Formula reading, four items.
Mass before and after reaction, open flask then sealed with a balloon; record to 0.01 g.
Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed. Account for the missing mass as escaped carbon dioxide.
Three scenarios: predict whether recorded mass rises, falls or stays the same, and explain.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: Where did the missing mass go?
Why does magnesium appear to gain mass when burned?
support: Atom-counting counters to model before and after.
challenge: Given masses of two reactants and one product, calculate the mass of the second product.
lessons.homework: Explain why a burning candle appears to lose mass but the system does not.
lessons.exitTicket: State the law of conservation of mass in one sentence.

lessons.title: Modelling substances
objectives: Build and interpret molecular models of elements and compounds
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of a model
retrieval: State the law of conservation of mass

sequence.detail: Four questions spanning Lessons 1 to 4.
Molecular model kits: build eight named substances from formulae, then a partner names them from the model.
Evaluate the kit as a model: what it shows well (ratio, bonding) and what it misleads on (size, colour, motion, spacing).
Written evaluation of the model against two criteria.

keyQuestions: What does this model get wrong about a real molecule?
Why do chemists still use it?
support: Formula cards with atom counts already tallied.
challenge: Build and compare a giant structure (silicon dioxide) with a simple molecule and describe the difference.
lessons.homework: Draw and label four of the models built, with formulae.
lessons.exitTicket: Give one strength and one limitation of a ball-and-stick model.

lessons.title: Review and assessment

sequence.detail: Knowledge organiser self-quizzing, look-cover-write-check.
20-mark quiz.
Peer mark against a visualised mark scheme; whole-class reteach of the weakest item.

support: Knowledge organiser available during self-quizzing but not during the quiz.
challenge: Write three exam-style questions with mark schemes for a partner.
lessons.homework: Green-pen corrections for every mark dropped.
lessons.exitTicket: Which symbol or formula rule will you practise this week?
